newsitem.title: UK: Pope could face surgical complications.
newsitem.headline: Pope could face surgical complications.

text.p: An operation to remove Pope John Paul's appendix should be straightforward, even for a man of his age and medical history, doctors say. But there could be more serious complications.
The 76-year-old Pontiff is having the operation because occasional inflammation of the appendix has been the cause of three mild "intestinal fevers" he has suffered since Christmas, the Vatican said.
It will be the sixth time the Pope has been in hospital since he took office in 1978. If all goes well, he should be out of hospital in a week and back at work in a month.

The appendix, a largely useless intestinal organ, can be removed either by means of a conventional surgical incision in the lower right-hand quadrant of the abdomen or by keyhole surgery, a technique in use since about 1980.

But what has aroused doctors' suspicions is the fact that it is unusual for a person as old as the pope to have his appendix out, and the operation is mostly carried out as an emergency procedure as a result of acute appendicitis.

The delay in operating on the Pope has led doctors to speculate that he may be suffering from a "grumbling appendix", or that he may have a recurrence of a 1992 tumour. The Vatican has denied there are any signs of another tumour.

The Pope had major abdominal surgery twice in 1981 after he was shot by a would-be assassin and again in 1992 to remove a colonic tumour. He had a hip replacement in 1994 and dislocated a shoulder in 1993.
"It may be that he has got a grumbling appendix," Michael McMahon, professor of surgery at Britain's University of Leeds, told Reuters. "It is also possible that he has a tumour."
"It could mean major surgery," said Charles Collins, a consultant surgeon and a member of the council of the Royal College of Surgeons.
"If it is just the appendix that is removed, then that is straightforward. My concern is that he has got another tumour in the colon."

Doctors estimate the chances of the Pope dying during an operation to remove his appendix at about one in 1,000. If surgeons have to remove a colonic tumour, the odds narrow to about one or two in 100.
Scars left by the surgery after the Pope was shot could also make any subsequent operation more difficult.
"The older they are, the greater the risk," said McMahon. "But generally speaking the risk to life from removal of the appendix, with modern medicine, even at the age of 76, is very low."
Up to eight people in every hundred have had their appendix removed.
McMahon said that, if patients thought to have appendicitis are operated on and found to have a healthy appendix, it must still be removed.

This is because the incision leaves a telltake scar and, if the appendix is left in, doctors will think it has been taken out and assume, probably wrongly, that any future pain cannot be caused by appendicitis.
